blocks.text: From the fly Beel-zebub, the god of the Ekronites, takes his name, 2 Reg. I, 2. The LXX render μυῖαν Θεὸν Ἀκκαρὼν [myian Theon Akkarōn], the fly, the god of Ekron. Many of the ancients follow this. Thus Josephus, book 9, chapter 1, relates that Ahaziah sent πρὸς τὸν Ἀκκάρων Θεὸν μυῖαν, τοῦτο γὰρ ἦν ὄνομα τῷ θεῷ [pros ton Akkarōn Theon myian, touto gar ēn onoma tō theō], to the god of Ekron, the fly, for that was the name of the god. And in Suidas, under the word Ἠλίας [Ēlias], an ancient writer says of the same Ahaziah: Ἐχρήσατο μυίᾳ τῶν ἐν Ἀκκάρων εἰδώλῳ [Echrēsato myia tōn en Akkarōn eidōlō], He consulted the fly, the idol of the Ekronites. Alluding to this, Nazianzen in his fourth Oration says: [III, 347] Οὐδὲ ζητήσουσι μυῖαν Θεὸν Ἀκκαρὼν, ἢ εἴ τι ταύτης ἐστὶ γελοιότερον [Oude zētēsousi myian Theon Akkarōn, ē ei ti tautēs esti geloioteron]. Nor will they any longer seek the fly, the god of Ekron, or any other deity more ridiculous than that. The Greek Fathers, that is, think that this god was worshipped under the image of a fly. Theodoret on this passage: Τί μυσαρώτερον μυίας; ἀλλ᾽ ὅμως τὴν εἰκόνα ταύτης Θεὸν ἀνηγόρευσαν [Ti mysarōteron myias? all᾽ homōs tēn eikona tautēs Theon anēgoreusan]. What is more loathsome than a fly? Yet they declared its image to be a god. And a little later: Ἣν ζῶσαν ταῖς ῥιπίσιν ἐλαύνουσι, ταύτης τὸν τύπον Θεὸν προσηγόρευσαν [Hēn zōsan tais rhipisin elaunousi, tautēs ton typon Theon prosēgoreusan]· The creature which, when alive, they drive away with fly-whisks, its figure they called a god. Following them, Philastrius, in his Catalogue of the heretics who lived before Christ, lists the Muscaccaronites, who, he says, worship a fly in the city of Ekron. Procopius too ascribes to this same god the image of a fly. Yet he doubts whether it was the name of a demon, or of an old woman raised to the gods. This fancy is refuted by the Hebrew name בעל־זבוב, Beel-zebub, which is compounded of masculine words. I prefer therefore to follow the Latins, for whom Beel-zebub is not, in the nominative, the god fly, but, with a genitive, the god or lord of the fly. Augustine, Tractate 1 on John: BEEL-ZEBUB is said to be interpreted prince of flies. Jerome on Ecclesiastes, chapter 10: From these flies the prince of demons is also called BEEL-ZEBUB, which is interpreted either idol of flies, or man of flies, or having flies. And on Matthew, chapter 10: Beel-zebub is the idol of Ekron, which in the book of Kings is called the idol of the fly. The Book of Names, on John: BEEL-ZEBUB, having flies, or man of flies. Isidore, Origins, book 8, chapter 11: BEEL-ZEBUB [col. 500] was the idol of Ekron, which is interpreted man of flies. I would rather say god, or lord, or prince of flies, as in Augustine. For בעל Baal, when it is the name of an idol, does not mean man, but god or lord. Nor is the reason for the name obscure, since the Greeks too had a god Μυιώδης [Myiōdēs], or Μυίαγρος [Myiagros], or Ἀπόμυιος [Apomyios], whether he was Jupiter, or Hercules, or some other god, so called from driving away flies ^{(3)}. On this matter the passages of the ancients are explicit. Pliny [III, 348], book 10, chapter 28: The Eleans (invoke) the god Myiagrus when a multitude of flies brings pestilence ^{(4)}; and they die at once, on the day on which a sacrifice has been offered to him. Others read: once a sacrifice has been offered to that god. And book 29, chapter 6: No animal (the fly) is thought less teachable or of less understanding; all the more wonderful is it that at the sacred Olympic games, when a bull has been sacrificed to the god whom they call Myiodes, clouds of them depart out of that territory. Pausanias in the Arcadica, on the festival of the Aliphereans: Ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ πανηγύρει Μυιάγρῳ προθύουσιν, ἐπευχόμενοί τε κατὰ τῶν ἱερείων τῷ ἥρωϊ, καὶ ἐπικαλούμενοι τὸν Μυίαγρον. Καὶ σφισι ταῦτα δράσασιν, οὐδὲν ἔτι ἀνιαρόν εἰσιν αἱ μυῖαι [En tautē tē panēgyrei Myiagrō prothyousin, epeuchomenoi te kata tōn hiereiōn tō hērōi, kai epikaloumenoi ton Myiagron. Kai sphisi tauta drasasin, ouden eti aniaron eisin hai myiai]. At that festival they first of all offer sacrifice to Myiagrus; and when they have prayed to the hero over the victims and invoked the name of Myiagrus, after doing this the flies no longer trouble them. And in the first book of the Eliaca: Φασὶ δὲ Ἡρακλεῖ τῷ Ἀλκμήνης, θύοντι ἐν Ὀλυμπίᾳ, δι᾽ ὄχλου μάλιστα γενέσθαι τὰς μυίας. ἐξευρόντα οὖν αὐτὸν, ἢ καὶ ὑπ᾽ ἄλλου διδαχθέντα, Ἀπομυίῳ θῦσαι Διῒ, καὶ οὕτως ἀποτραπῆναι τὰς μυίας περὰν τοῦ Ἀλφειοῦ· Λέγονται δὲ κατὰ ταῦτα καὶ Ἠλεῖοι θύειν τῷ Ἀπομυίῳ Διῒ ἐξελαύνοντι τῆς Ἠλείας Ὀλυμπίας τὰς μυίας [Phasi de Hēraklei tō Alkmēnēs, thyonti en Olympia, di᾽ ochlou malista genesthai tas myias. exeuronta oun auton, ē kai hyp᾽ allou didachthenta, Apomyiō thysai Dii, kai houtōs apotrapēnai tas myias peran tou Alpheiou; Legontai de kata tauta kai Ēleioi thyein tō Apomyiō Dii exelaunonti tēs Ēleias Olympias tas myias]· They also say that when Hercules, son of Alcmene, was sacrificing at Olympia, the flies caused him very great trouble. So, either by his own discovery or on another's advice, he sacrificed to Jupiter Apomyius (as if to say the driver-away of flies), and thus the flies were routed across the Alpheus. And accordingly the Eleans are said to sacrifice to Jupiter Apomyius, who drives the flies away from Olympia in Elis ^{(5)}. Of this same rite Aelian says much in the History [III, 349], book 5, chapter 17, and book 11, chapter 8. So does Antiphanes the comic poet in Athenaeus, book 1, chapter 5. Clement too in the Protrepticus: Ἀπομυίῳ Διῒ θύουσιν Ἠλεῖοι, Ῥωμαῖοι δὲ Ἀπομυίῳ Ἡρακλεῖ [Apomyiō Dii thyousin Ēleioi, Rhōmaioi de Apomyiō Hēraklei]. And Solinus, chapter 1, on the shrine of Hercules at Rome in the Forum Boarium: By divine power it is entered neither by dogs nor by flies. For when he was giving a distribution of sacrificial meat to the worshippers, he is said to have invoked the god Myiagrus. Pliny reports the same in part, book 10, chapter 29: At Rome neither flies nor dogs enter the temple of Hercules in the Forum Boarium. So too at Paphos, περὶ τὰ θυρώματα τὰ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης [peri ta thyrōmata ta tēs Aphroditēs], around the doors of Venus (unless we should read περὶ τὰ θυσιάσματα [peri ta thysiasmata], around the sacrifices of Venus), there is no fly. So Apollonius records from Andron in the History of Marvels, 8. And at Leucas the flies, sated with ox blood, depart from the shrine of Apollo Actius, as is found in Aelian, History, book 11, chapter 8. Nor are flies found on the mountain of Crete, Carina, nine miles in circuit, if we believe Pliny, book 21, chapter 14. And the Jews report that some such miracle also occurred in the temple of God at Jerusalem, in Pirke Aboth, chapter 5, section 5. The words are לא נראה זבוב בבית המטבחים, No fly was seen in the house of slaughtering. If this is true, the devil, as usual, will have been God's ape in this respect. And just as Apollo at Athens was called PARNOPIUS, and Hercules on Mount Oeta CORNOPION, because of locusts driven away; and by the Erythraeans Ἰποκτόνος [Ipoktonos], because of the ἶπες [ipes] he killed, that is, the small worms by which vines are infested: so whatever god was believed to drive away flies, as in Greek μυίαγρος [myiagros], μυιώδης [myiōdēs] and ἀπόμυιος [apomyios], will in Hebrew have been called BEEL-ZEBUB, that [col. 501] is, lord of flies. Such he was believed to have shown himself, by removing and driving them away from his sacrifices. I therefore think this was the true name of that idol. Nor do I agree with a great man ^{(6)}, who thinks that he was called by his worshippers בעל זבחים Beel-zebachim, that is, god of sacrifices, which the Israelites in contempt twisted into בעלזבוב Beel-zebub, that is, lord of the fly. For, to say nothing of the fact that zebub and zebachim are words so unlike that a play on them seems hardly to have been sought; nor that it is likely that any god took his name from the victims offered, since it was common to all to be worshipped by the offering of victims: it is certain that Ahaziah was in earnest when he said, Go, and inquire of Beel-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I shall recover from this sickness. For Ahaziah will not have mocked the god whom, in his sickness, he ordered to be consulted about his recovery. I therefore think the name Beel-zebub was in use among the Philistines as much as among the Israelites [III, 350] ^{(7)}. But since in the Gospel we read Beel-zebul, with L at the end, as if derived from the word זבל zebel, which means dung, I should think the later Jews altered [III, 351] the name, so as to relegate Beel-zebub in this way among the dung gods ^{(8)}. Yet this is not necessary, since in those languages a final B is sometimes changed into L. Thus the mouth of the Arabian gulf is commonly called Babelmandel for the Arabic باب المندب [Bāb al-Mandab] Bab-elmandab. And the nablium, in Spanish rabel, is in Arabic رباب [rabāb] rebab. In the same way Beel-zebul could be said for Beel-zebub.
